content.thinking:
This is a social norms intervention showing people that 76% of Americans trust climate scientists at least somewhat, likely correcting an underestimation bias. I'm recalling that similar descriptive-norm corrections in climate research tend to shift perceived norms substantially but produce only modest changes (roughly 1-4 points on 100-point scales) in actual trust or attitudes.

I'm settling on modest positive estimates across the board: trust measures around +2, secondary outcomes like funding perceptions, institutional trust, and policy support in the +0.6 to +1.0 range, with tiny effects on donation and newsletter behavior. I'm weighing the possibility of backfire from polarization skepticism but leaning toward the Pew-sourced, quantitative framing being broadly credible enough to avoid backlash, keeping my final numbers conservative and modest overall.

content.text: {"reasoning_summary": "This is a descriptive-norm correction with interactive misperception feedback: respondents first guess the share of Americans trusting climate scientists (most will guess well below 76%, given perceived polarization), then receive a credible Pew-sourced correction plus a 'shared values' frame. Mechanisms are conformity/social proof and a credibility inference ('if most people trust them, they are probably trustworthy'), which act most directly on the trust items — particularly trust_post, which is worded almost identically to the norm statement. Norm-correction studies typically produce large shifts in perceived norms but only modest shifts in personal attitudes (roughly 1–3 points on 100-point scales), and downstream belief/concern/policy items are further attenuated because belief and concern are strongly crystallized and anchored on pre-treatment answers. Some conservatives may find the 76% figure implausible or react against a perceived consensus cue, capping the average effect; hence I center trust effects near +2, distrust slightly negative, secondary attitudes under +1.5, self-reported behavior smaller still, and incentivized behaviors (donation, newsletter) at near-zero fractions.", "ates": {"trust_multidimensional": 1.9, "trust_post": 2.3, "distrust_post": -1.3, "funding_perceptions": 0.8, "policy_role_mean": 1.1, "inst_trust_mean": 1.1, "belief_post": 0.8, "concern_mean": 0.9, "policy_general": 1.0, "policy_specific_mean": 0.8, "behavior_mean": 0.6, "donation_ams": 0.05, "newsletter_signup": 0.005}}

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This is a descriptive-norm correction with interactive misperception feedback: respondents first guess the share of Americans trusting climate scientists (most will guess well below 76%, given perceived polarization), then receive a credible Pew-sourced correction plus a 'shared values' frame. Mechanisms are conformity/social proof and a credibility inference ('if most people trust them, they are probably trustworthy'), which act most directly on the trust items — particularly trust_post, which is worded almost identically to the norm statement. Norm-correction studies typically produce large shifts in perceived norms but only modest shifts in personal attitudes (roughly 1–3 points on 100-point scales), and downstream belief/concern/policy items are further attenuated because belief and concern are strongly crystallized and anchored on pre-treatment answers. Some conservatives may find the 76% figure implausible or react against a perceived consensus cue, capping the average effect; hence I center trust effects near +2, distrust slightly negative, secondary attitudes under +1.5, self-reported behavior smaller still, and incentivized behaviors (donation, newsletter) at near-zero fractions.
